Q: Why do indices behave differently than setting to a variable in bash loops over arrays that contain quotes and spaces? A:

Arrays, sub-array and indexes under bash

I mostly prefer to use read -a or mapfile to populate an array from the result of splitting a variable, instead of array=($variable) syntax:

samples=("one 1 uno" "two 2 dos" "three 3 tres")
for index in ${!samples[@]}; do
    IFS=' ' read -ra fields <<<"${samples[index]}"
    printf 'Index:  %2d -> String: %-16s -> Array: [%s]\n' \
            "$index" "${samples[index]@Q}" "${fields[*]@Q}"
done

As wjandrea' comment correctly pointed out: Using array=($variable) syntax not only fail if fields do contain space, but will expand glob whenever possible!

Note the use of * instead of @ for printing array as a single string!

Index:   0 -> String: 'one 1 uno'      -> Array: ['one' '1' 'uno']
Index:   1 -> String: 'two 2 dos'      -> Array: ['two' '2' 'dos']
Index:   2 -> String: 'three 3 tres'   -> Array: ['three' '3' 'tres']

To strictly match your output:

for index in ${!samples[@]}; do
    IFS=' ' read -ra fields <<<"${samples[index]}"
    printf '%d ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n   %s\n   just the first: %s\n' \
            "$index" "${samples[index]}" "${fields[0]}"
done

0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   one 1 uno
   just the first: one
1 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   two 2 dos
   just the first: two
2 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   three 3 tres
   just the first: three

One step further

Or why I prefer not to use array=($variable) syntax

If fields in my array could contain spaces, I will use, for sample, tab as first array separator:

samples=($'one\t1\tuno' $'two\t2\tdos' $'third entry\t3 th\ttercera entrada')
for index in ${!samples[@]}; do
    IFS=$'\t' read -ra fields <<<"${samples[index]}"
    printf '%d ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n   %s\n   just the first: %s\n' \
            "$index" "${samples[index]}" "${fields[0]}"
done

0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   one  1   uno
   just the first: one
1 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   two  2   dos
   just the first: two
2 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   third entry  3 th    tercera entrada
   just the first: third entry

Without loop

By using a temporary string as format print:

samples=($'one\t1\tuno' $'two\t2\tdos' $'third entry\t3 th\ttercera entrada')
printf -v tmpStr '%d ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n   %%s\n   just the first: %%%%s\n' \
        "${!samples[@]}"
printf -v tmpStr "$tmpStr" "${samples[@]}"
printf "$tmpStr" "${samples[@]%%$'\t'*}"

0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   one  1   uno
   just the first: one
1 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   two  2   dos
   just the first: two
2 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
   third entry  3 th    tercera entrada
   just the first: third entry

Q: How to install Mermaid to render flowcharts in markdown? A:

If you're looking for a browser-based Mermaid editor, there are a few good options.

I built one because I wanted something lightweight that opens instantly without any setup.

Link - Mermaid

Features include:

• Live preview while typing

• Flowcharts

• Sequence diagrams

• Class diagrams

• ER diagrams

• Gantt charts

• Copy and export support

For local development, Mermaid CLI or the VS Code extension are still great choices. But if you just need to quickly test or edit Mermaid syntax, an online editor is usually much faster.

(Disclosure: I'm the creator of the linked editor.)
